--- title: "Week 12: Logistic Regression" subtitle: "Date: November 12, 2026" footer: "[course-website](https://dharaden.github.io/psyc640/)" logo: "images/640_hex.png" format: revealjs: theme: [default, brand, clean.scss] multiplex: false transition: fade slide-number: true incremental: false chalkboard: true overview: false scrollable: true code-line-numbers: true auto-stretch: false editor: visual execute: echo: true freeze: auto editor_options: chunk_output_type: console --- ## Today... **When the outcome is yes or no** - Why `lm()` breaks when Y is 0 or 1 - Probability → odds → log-odds (the one new idea today) - `glm(..., family = binomial)`, and turning its output into odds ratios - Predicted probabilities: the way to *explain* a logistic model - 👻 Who believes in ghosts? . . . ::: callout-tip ## The plan for class | | | |---------------------|-----------------------| | Lecture | \~50 min | | 🚿 Activity | \~20 min | | ☕ Break | | | 📂 **M2 work time** | **the rest of class** | M2 is due **Sunday 11/15**. Bring your questions. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(rio) library(here) library(broom) library(easystats) options(scipen = 999) cah <- import(here("files", "data", "CAH.csv")) %>% mutate(across(where(is.character), ~ na_if(.x, ""))) ``` ::: **The data:** Cards Against Humanity's *Pulse of the Nation* poll (2017). 1,000 U.S. adults, real survey questions, and some less serious ones. # Part 1: Why Not Just `lm()`? ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## A yes/no outcome So far every outcome has been a number on a scale. Lots of outcomes in psychology are **binary**: - Diagnosed or not - Relapsed or not - Completed the study or dropped out - Answered the item correctly or not . . . Code it **1 = the thing happened** and **0 = it didn't**. Then the mean of the 0s and 1s is the **proportion** of 1s, which is a probability. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## What happens with `lm()`? A made-up class of 200: hours studied and whether they passed the exam. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} set.seed(1112) exam <- tibble(hours = runif(200, 0, 20), passed = rbinom(200, 1, plogis(-6 + 0.6 * hours))) lpm <- lm(passed ~ hours, data = exam) range(predict(lpm)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] -0.1555193 1.1928485 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot(exam, aes(hours, passed)) + geom_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.03, alpha = 0.4) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "#C8102E") + geom_hline(yintercept = c(0, 1), linetype = "dashed") + labs(x = "Hours studied", y = "Passed (1) or not (0)") + theme_bw(base_size = 15) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-12_logistic-reg_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=75%} ::: ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Three problems ::: incremental 1. **Impossible predictions.** A student who studied 0 hours has a "probability" of passing of −16%. Someone at 20 hours: 119%. 2. **The residuals can't be normal.** For any *X*, the residual can only take two values (1 − *Ŷ* or 0 − *Ŷ*). 3. **The variance isn't constant.** It's largest near *p* = .5 and shrinks toward 0 and 1. (Week 10: heteroscedasticity, built in.) ::: . . . We need a model whose predictions **stay between 0 and 1** and bend near the edges. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The S-curve ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true"} ggplot(exam, aes(hours, passed)) + geom_jitter(width = 0, height = 0.03, alpha = 0.4) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "gray60", linetype = "dashed") + geom_smooth(method = "glm", method.args = list(family = binomial), se = FALSE, color = "#C8102E", linewidth = 1.3) + labs(x = "Hours studied", y = "Probability of passing") + theme_bw(base_size = 15) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-12_logistic-reg_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){width=75%} ::: ::: Same data. The red curve is a **logistic regression**: never below 0, never above 1, steepest in the middle. # Part 2: Probability, Odds, Log-Odds ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Three ways to say the same thing | Probability *p* | Odds = *p* / (1 − *p*) | Log-odds = ln(odds) | |:---------------:|:----------------------:|:-------------------:| | .10 | 0.11 (1 to 9) | −2.20 | | .25 | 0.33 (1 to 3) | −1.10 | | **.50** | **1** (even) | **0** | | .75 | 3 (3 to 1) | 1.10 | | .90 | 9 (9 to 1) | 2.20 | . . . - **Probability** is stuck between 0 and 1. - **Odds** run from 0 to ∞. - **Log-odds** run from −∞ to +∞, like any regression outcome. So logistic regression fits a **straight line on the log-odds scale**: $$ \ln\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right) = b_0 + b_1 X_1 + b_2 X_2 + \cdots $$ ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## A room of 10 people 👻 Ten people answer "Do you believe in ghosts?" ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Room A 👻👻👻👻👻👻👻👻🙅🙅 | | | |-----------------|--------------------------| | **Probability** | 8 of 10 = **.80** | | **Odds** | 8 believers to 2 = **4** | | **Log-odds** | ln(4) = **+1.39** | ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ### Room B 🙅🙅🙅🙅🙅🙅🙅🙅👻👻 | | | |-----------------|-----------------------------| | **Probability** | 2 of 10 = **.20** | | **Odds** | 2 believers to 8 = **0.25** | | **Log-odds** | ln(0.25) = **−1.39** | ::: ::::: . . . - **Odds** are a head count: "4 believers for every non-believer." - Room B is Room A **flipped**, but the odds (4 vs. 0.25) don't look like mirror images. - The **log-odds** do: +1.39 vs. −1.39. Zero is the 5-and-5 room. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Why bother with the log? Because **adding** on the log-odds scale is **multiplying** the odds. | Log-odds | | Odds | | Probability | |:---------------:|:---:|:-------------:|:---:|:-----------:| | 0 | | 1 | | .50 | | 0 **+ 0.69** | → | 1 **× 2** = 2 | → | .67 | | 0.69 **+ 0.69** | → | 2 **× 2** = 4 | → | .80 | | 1.39 **+ 0.69** | → | 4 **× 2** = 8 | → | .89 | . . . - A regression line **adds** a fixed amount for each unit of *X*. That's the log-odds column. - exp(0.69) = 2, so each step **doubles** the odds. That's the odds ratio. - The **probability** goes up by less and less each step: +.17, then +.13, then +.09. It can't pass 1. ::: callout-important One coefficient, three readings: **+0.69** in log-odds = **× 2** in odds = **"it depends where you start"** in probability. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Turn the dial 🎛️ ```{=html}

``` Try 0, then ±1.39 (the two rooms), then ±4. Each step of 1 near the middle moves the probability a lot; out near the edges it barely moves. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The catch Coefficients come out in **log-odds**, and nobody thinks in log-odds. . . . So we translate: | Scale | How to get there | Read it as | |----|----|----| | Log-odds | what `glm()` gives you | sign and *p*-value only | | Odds ratio | `exp(b)` | "the odds are multiplied by \_\_\_" | | Probability | `predict(..., type = "response")` | "a \_\_\_ has a \_\_% chance" | . . . ::: callout-important Odds ratio = 1 means no effect. **Above 1:** higher odds. **Below 1:** lower odds. An OR of 0.40 means the odds are 60% lower, **not** that the probability is. ::: # Part 3: Who Believes in Ghosts? 👻 ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The question > "Do you believe in ghosts?" (Yes / No) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ghosts <- cah %>% filter(gender %in% c("Female", "Male"), !is.na(ghosts)) %>% mutate(ghost = if_else(ghosts == "Yes", 1, 0), # 1 = believes gender = factor(gender, levels = c("Female", "Male"), labels = c("Woman", "Man"))) ghosts %>% summarise(n = n(), prop_believe = mean(ghost)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` n prop_believe 1 946 0.3773784 ``` ::: ::: . . . About 38% believe. (I dropped the 28 people who answered "Other" for gender. With *n* = 28, the estimate would be very noisy. In your own work, make that decision before you see the results, and report it.) ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## `glm()`: one new argument ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_age <- glm(ghost ~ age, data = ghosts, family = binomial) tidy(m_age) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 term estimate std.error statistic p.value 1 (Intercept) 0.0292 0.211 0.139 0.890 2 age -0.0109 0.00412 -2.63 0.00842 ``` ::: ::: . . . - `family = binomial` is what makes it logistic. Leave it off and you've fit `lm()` again. - The age coefficient is **−0.011** in log-odds: older people are less likely to believe, *p* = .008. - What does −0.011 log-odds per year **mean**? Nothing intuitive. Translate. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Odds ratio for age ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} model_parameters(m_age, exponentiate = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Parameter | Odds Ratio | SE | 95% CI | z | p ------------------------------------------------------------------ (Intercept) | 1.03 | 0.22 | [0.68, 1.56] | 0.14 | 0.890 age | 0.99 | 4.08e-03 | [0.98, 1.00] | -2.63 | 0.008 ``` ::: ::: . . . **OR = 0.989** per year: each year of age multiplies the odds of believing by 0.989, about **1% lower odds per year**. . . . Per year is tiny. Per **decade**: exp(10 × −0.0109) = 0.90, so **10% lower odds** for every 10 years older. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## A categorical predictor: gender Before the model, the 2 × 2 table: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ghosts %>% group_by(gender) %>% summarise(n = n(), believe = sum(ghost), p = mean(ghost)) %>% mutate(odds = p / (1 - p)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 2 × 5 gender n believe p odds 1 Woman 476 232 0.487 0.951 2 Man 470 125 0.266 0.362 ``` ::: ::: . . . Odds ratio by hand: **0.362 / 0.951 = 0.38**. Men have about 38% of the odds that women do. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_gender <- glm(ghost ~ gender, data = ghosts, family = binomial) model_parameters(m_gender, exponentiate = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Parameter | Odds Ratio | SE | 95% CI | z | p ---------------------------------------------------------------- (Intercept) | 0.95 | 0.09 | [0.79, 1.14] | -0.55 | 0.582 gender [Man] | 0.38 | 0.05 | [0.29, 0.50] | -6.94 | < .001 ``` ::: ::: Same number. **The odds ratio is just a ratio of two groups' odds.** The intercept (0.95) is the reference group's odds: women. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Both predictors ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_both <- glm(ghost ~ age + gender, data = ghosts, family = binomial) model_parameters(m_both, exponentiate = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Parameter | Odds Ratio | SE | 95% CI | z | p -------------------------------------------------------------------- (Intercept) | 1.88 | 0.44 | [1.19, 2.98] | 2.70 | 0.007 age | 0.99 | 4.23e-03 | [0.98, 0.99] | -3.17 | 0.002 gender [Man] | 0.37 | 0.05 | [0.28, 0.48] | -7.14 | < .001 ``` ::: ::: . . . Same "holding constant" logic as multiple regression: - **Age:** holding gender constant, each year multiplies the odds of believing by 0.99. - **Gender:** holding age constant, men have **0.37 times** the odds of believing that women do (63% lower odds). ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Follow one person through the model ::: {.cell} ::: A **25-year-old woman.** Plug her into the model, one scale at a time: | Step | Woman, 25 | Man, 25 | |:---|:--:|:--:| | **Log-odds** = *b*~0~ + *b*~age~ × 25 (+ *b*~man~) | 0.630 + (-0.0136 × 25) = **0.29** | 0.29 + (-1.00) = **-0.71** | | **Odds** = e^log-odds^ | e\^0.29\^ = **1.34** | e\^-0.71\^ = **0.49** | | **Probability** = odds / (1 + odds) | 1.34 / 2.34 = **.57** | 0.49 / 1.49 = **.33** | . . . - On the **log-odds** scale, being a man **subtracts 1.00**. - On the **odds** scale, it **multiplies by 0.37**: 1.34 × 0.37 = 0.49. That's the odds ratio. - On the **probability** scale, it's .57 → .33. That is **not** .57 × 0.37. . . . `plogis()` does the last two steps in one go: `plogis(0.29)` = 0.57. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Same odds ratio, different probability change Men have 0.37 times the odds. What that does to the **probability** depends on where you start: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} | Woman's probability | Same-age man (× OR on the odds) | Change (percentage points) | |:-------------------:|:-------------------------------:|:--------------------------:| | .05 | .02 | -3 | | .20 | .08 | -12 | | .50 | .27 | -23 | | .80 | .59 | -21 | | .95 | .87 | -8 | ::: ::: . . . The odds ratio is the **same in every row**. The change in probability is biggest near .50 and tiny near 0 or 1, because that's where the S-curve is steepest. ::: callout-tip This is why a Results section reports the **odds ratio** (one number that's true everywhere), and the Discussion uses **predicted probabilities** at values of *X* that matter. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The best way to explain it: predicted probabilities Odds ratios are for the Results section. **Probabilities** are for humans. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} new_people <- expand_grid(age = c(25, 65), gender = c("Woman", "Man")) new_people %>% mutate(p_believe = predict(m_both, newdata = new_people, type = "response")) %>% mutate(p_believe = round(p_believe, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 4 × 3 age gender p_believe 1 25 Woman 0.57 2 25 Man 0.33 3 65 Woman 0.44 4 65 Man 0.22 ``` ::: ::: . . . A 25-year-old woman: **57%**. A 65-year-old man: **22%**. ::: callout-warning `type = "response"` matters. Leave it off and `predict()` returns **log-odds**. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Plot the probabilities ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} augment(m_both, type.predict = "response") %>% ggplot(aes(age, .fitted, color = gender)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1.3) + labs(x = "Age", y = "Predicted probability of believing in ghosts", color = NULL) + ylim(0, 1) + theme_bw(base_size = 15) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-12_logistic-reg_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: The lines look almost straight here because the probabilities stay in the middle of the range. The S only shows up near 0 and 1. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Did gender earn its place? Last week's block comparison works here too, with one change: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} anova(m_age, m_both, test = "Chisq") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Deviance Table Model 1: ghost ~ age Model 2: ghost ~ age + gender Resid. Df Resid. Dev Df Deviance Pr(>Chi) 1 944 1246.9 2 943 1193.8 1 53.136 0.0000000000003113 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: . . . Logistic regression has no *F* test. It compares **deviance** (the logistic version of leftover error) with a χ² test. Adding gender reduced deviance by 53.1, χ²(1) = 53.14, *p* \< .001. . . . ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} r2(m_both) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # R2 for Logistic Regression Tjur's R2: 0.063 ``` ::: ::: There's no true *R*² either. **Tjur's *R*²** = .063: the gap between the average predicted probability for believers and for non-believers. Small, so most of what decides who believes in ghosts isn't in this model. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Writing it up ::: {.cell} ::: > We used logistic regression to predict belief in ghosts (1 = yes) from age and gender (*N* = 946; 37.7% believed). Holding age constant, men had lower odds of believing than women, OR = 0.37, 95% CI [0.28, 0.48], *p* \< .001. Each additional year of age was associated with slightly lower odds, OR = 0.987, 95% CI [0.978, 0.995], *p* = .002. For example, the model predicts a 57% probability of believing for a 25-year-old woman and 22% for a 65-year-old man. . . . ::: callout-tip Report the **odds ratio with its CI**, then give at least one **predicted probability** so readers can tell how big the effect is. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Three ways to get it wrong ::: incremental 1. **Not checking which level is 1.** If R treats "No" as the outcome, every odds ratio flips. Always create the 0/1 variable yourself and say what 1 means. 2. **Reading log-odds as probabilities.** "−0.011" doesn't mean 1.1 percentage points. Exponentiate, or predict. 3. **Treating an odds ratio as a risk ratio.** OR = 0.37 doesn't mean men are 37% as *likely* to believe. Their probability is 27% vs. 49%, a ratio of 0.55. Odds ratios exaggerate when the outcome is common. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Logistic vs. linear, side by side | | Linear | Logistic | |:----------------|:----------------|:-------------------------------------| | Outcome | Continuous | Binary (0/1) | | R | `lm(y ~ x)` | `glm(y ~ x, family = binomial)` | | Coefficient | Change in *Y* | Change in **log-odds** | | Easier to read | *b* itself | **exp(*b*)** = odds ratio | | Compare models | `anova()` → *F* | `anova(test = "Chisq")` → χ² | | Fit | *R*² | Tjur's *R*² (or another pseudo-*R*²) | | Explain it with | Predicted *Y* | **Predicted probability** | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## 💻 Your Turn: 🚿 Is It Acceptable? ::: callout-tip **\~20 min** · Pairs · Same CAH data ::: > "Is it acceptable to pee in the shower?" Who says yes? Age, gender, and a predicted probability for two people. [Open the activity](../class-activities/wk12_logistic.html){.button target="_blank"} # ☕ Break ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## 📂 M2 Work Time **Due Sunday 11/15.** Use the rest of class. I'll come around. ::: callout-note ## M2 checklist (from Week 11) - [ ] `split.qmd` run: the explore sample is the **only** file you open - [ ] Every variable audited against the codebook, with the codes it doesn't explain listed - [ ] Missing-data codes recoded with `na_if()`, each with a one-line reason - [ ] Participant flow: *n* after each exclusion - [ ] `analytic` built, complete on **every** variable in **any** planned model - [ ] Complete vs. incomplete cases compared on your outcome ::: . . . **Is your outcome binary?** Then today's model is your model. Ask me about it while you're here. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## For next time 📂 **M2**, due **Sunday 11/15** 📋 **Lab 11: Logistic Regression**, due **Tuesday 11/17 at 11:59pm** 📖 Readings for **Mixed/Multilevel Models**: - Chapter 8.8 — MSR - Chapter 15.8 — ST 💾 **Class Check** next week

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
